aimTitle: Explore website design skills and techniques to meet client requirements
board: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Extended Certificate in IT (AAQ)

checklist.name: Creating wireframes: wireframing tools (sketching on paper, graphic design software like Photoshop/Illustrator, UX design software like Figma/Adobe XD, dedicated wireframing apps like Balsamiq), wireframing techniques (hierarchy of page elements, balance of content, grouping elements, aligning elements, accurate dimensions)
Wireframes are low-fidelity layouts: boxes and placeholder text showing where elements go — not final designs. They show structure, not style.
Design ideas: visual style (colour palette, branding, typography), visual representations/mockups of the web pages (high-fidelity designs showing colours, images, fonts)
Reviewing fitness for purpose: quality (clarity, detail), user experience, meeting client requirements — review your designs, get feedback, and make improvements

Creating assets: writing headlines and copy (short sentences, short paragraphs, avoiding jargon, appropriate mode of address for the target audience); visual assets (image editing techniques like cropping and resizing, image manipulation like colour correction and layers, vector graphic drawing like logos)
Sourcing assets: written copy (write your own), stock images (e.g. royalty-free sites like Unsplash, Pixabay), icons, video — always check licences and credit sources

Preparing assets: trimming video (cut to relevant clips), compression (reduce file size for faster loading), file formats (choose the right format: JPG for photos, PNG for graphics with transparency, GIF/WebP for animations, MP4 for video — keep files under 1MB where possible)
Managing assets: logical folder structure (e.g. images/, css/, js/, video/), naming conventions (descriptive, consistent, no spaces — e.g. hero-banner.jpg, not 'IMG 3421.jpg')
Asset log: track every asset — name, source (own work or where downloaded from), and where it is used on the site

mcq.q: What is a wireframe?
options: A low-fidelity layout of a page showing the structure and placement of elements
The final finished design with colours and images
mcq.why: Wireframes are simple boxes and placeholders showing where elements go â€” structure first, style later.

mcq.q: Which is a wireframing tool or technique?
mcq.why: Wireframes can be sketched on paper, drawn in graphic design software, built in UX tools like Figma, or made in dedicated apps.

mcq.q: Which file format is usually best for a photographic image on a website?
mcq.why: JPG compresses photographs well. PNG suits graphics with transparency, SVG suits logos and icons, MP4 is for video.

mcq.q: Why compress and resize images before adding them to a website?
options: Large files slow the page down, hurting user experience and SEO
Because the HTML standard requires it
mcq.why: Large images increase loading time, which frustrates users (especially on mobile) and hurts search ranking. Compress to the size you actually use.

mcq.q: What is good practice for naming asset files?
options: Use the person who downloaded it as the name
Use consistent, descriptive names with no spaces (e.g. hero-banner.jpg)
Use random characters so they cannot clash
mcq.why: Descriptive names with dashes (hero-banner.jpg) are readable, consistent and don't break URLs â€” unlike 'IMG 3421.JPG'.

mcq.q: What is an asset log used for?
options: Tracking each asset â€” its name, source and where it appears on the site
mcq.why: An asset log shows where each asset came from (original work vs sourced, with credit) and how it's used â€” great evidence for the assignment.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a wireframe and a mockup?
options: A wireframe is low-fidelity structure; a mockup is a high-fidelity visual design
A mockup is a wireframe with no text
A wireframe is the final code
mcq.why: Wireframes show structure and layout in simple boxes; mockups add colour, images and typography to show the final look.

mcq.q: Why annotate a wireframe?
options: To explain the purpose of each element and how it meets the brief
mcq.why: Annotations show your thinking â€” why each element is there and how it meets client requirements â€” key evidence for the assignment.

mcq.q: What is a visual style?
options: The consistent look created by colour palette, typography, imagery and layout
mcq.why: The visual style ties together colour, fonts, images and spacing to create a cohesive, recognisable brand.

mcq.q: What is a brand identity?
options: The visual and verbal elements that represent a company (logo, colours, tone)
mcq.why: Brand identity includes the logo, colour palette, typography and tone of voice that make a company recognisable.

mcq.q: What does 'fitness for purpose' mean when reviewing a design?
options: Whether the design meets the client's requirements and works for the audience
mcq.why: Fitness for purpose asks: does this design actually do what the client and audience need? Review it against the brief.

mcq.q: Which file format is best for a logo with a transparent background?
mcq.why: PNG supports transparency, so a logo can sit on any background. SVG is even better for logos as it scales without losing quality.

mcq.q: What is a vector graphic?
options: An image made of paths that scales without losing quality (e.g. SVG)
mcq.why: Vector graphics use mathematical paths, so they stay sharp at any size â€” ideal for logos, icons and diagrams.

mcq.q: Why trim a video before adding it to a website?
options: To remove unnecessary footage and reduce file size
mcq.why: Trimming removes unwanted parts, reducing file size and loading time while keeping the content focused.

mcq.q: What is a folder structure for assets?
options: An organised set of folders (e.g. images/, css/, js/) to keep files tidy
mcq.why: A clear folder structure makes assets easy to find, maintain and reference â€” good practice and good evidence.

mcq.q: What is the difference between original and sourced assets?
options: Original assets are free; sourced are paid
Original assets you create yourself; sourced assets you obtain from elsewhere (with credit)
mcq.why: Creating your own assets shows skill; sourcing others requires credit and licence checks. Both are valid if managed properly.

mcq.q: What is a low-fidelity wireframe?
options: A rough, simple sketch showing basic structure without detail
mcq.why: Low-fidelity wireframes are quick, rough sketches (often on paper) to explore layout before investing in detail.

mcq.q: What is a high-fidelity mockup?
options: A detailed, polished design showing colours, fonts and images
mcq.why: High-fidelity mockups look close to the final site, showing the visual style in detail before coding.

mcq.q: What is a design review?
options: Assessing the design against the brief and audience to identify improvements
mcq.why: A design review compares the design to the brief and audience needs, identifying what to improve â€” key for the assignment.

mcq.q: What is image compression?
options: Reducing an image's file size while keeping acceptable quality
mcq.why: Compression reduces file size (faster loading) with minimal quality loss â€” essential for web performance.

mcq.q: What is a royalty-free image?
options: An image that is always free with no conditions
An image you can use without paying ongoing royalties, usually with a licence
mcq.why: Royalty-free means you pay once (or it's free) and can use it, but you should still check the licence terms.

quiz.q: Which order should you follow when planning a new site?
options: Requirements → sitemap → wireframes → visual design → build → test
quiz.why: Understand requirements first, then structure (sitemap), then layout (wireframes), then style (visual design), then build and test.

quiz.q: You created a logo in Illustrator. Which format preserves it as a scalable vector?
quiz.why: SVG is a vector format — it scales to any size without losing quality, perfect for logos and icons.

quiz.q: After designing wireframes, why should you review them against the client brief?
options: To check they meet client requirements and improve the designs
quiz.why: The spec requires reviewing fitness for purpose — checking quality, user experience and that the designs meet the client's requirements, then improving.

flashcards.back: A low-fidelity layout of a page showing structure and element placement (boxes, placeholders) — no colour or final styling. One per page for the assignment.
A high-fidelity representation of the page showing colours, images, typography and branding — how the page will actually look.
The consistent look of the site: colour palette, branding, typography choices applied across all pages.
Creating, sourcing, preparing and organising assets: writing copy, editing images, compressing, naming files consistently and logging sources.
A table tracking each asset — name, source (original work or where downloaded, with credit) and where it is used on the site.
Reviewing designs to check quality (clarity, detail), user experience and whether they meet the client's requirements — then improving them.

criteria.title: Designs and assets for the client brief

criteria.text: Produce adequate wireframes and visual designs for a specific purpose.
Use asset management techniques to develop assets that partially meet the client's requirements.
Produce mostly effective wireframes and visual designs for a specific purpose.
Use asset management techniques to develop assets that meet most of the client's requirements.
Make effective use of website design skills to develop designs and assets that comprehensively meet the client's requirements.

briefs.title: Retro Film Hub
briefs.scenario: Midnight Picture Show is a small independent cinema that hosts late-night screenings of classic films. They want a website that introduces young adults (17-23) to the films, stars and cultural moments of Hollywood's golden era.
briefs.purpose: To introduce a young adult audience to classic films and encourage them to visit the cinema.
briefs.targetAudience: 17- to 23-year-olds — many will have seen remakes or references to old films but never the originals.
mustIncludes: Three pages
Drop-down menus
Information about classic films (plot summaries, iconic stars, behind-the-scenes facts)
An accordion (e.g. 'Explore by genre or decade' with expandable sections)
External links to relevant websites (e.g. film archive sites, the cinema's ticketing site)
A form to request a specific film be screened
Modal images (click a film poster to view it enlarged)
Video content with controls (trailers — always embed from official sources)
Search functionality to find films
Accessibility features (alt text, high contrast, keyboard navigation, readable fonts)
briefs.typographyHint: Try a bold display font for headings to echo old cinema signage, with a clean sans-serif for body text.
briefs.colourHint: Golden-era Hollywood palette: deep burgundy, cream, gold and black — or teal and burnt orange for a vintage poster feel.

briefs.title: Community Action Charity
briefs.scenario: A non-profit organisation wants a website to create awareness of its activities and encourage teenagers to join as volunteers. It needs to show positive representations of its members and its work in the community.
briefs.purpose: To create awareness of the charity and encourage a teenage audience to get involved.
mustIncludes: Three pages
Information about the organisation (aims, activities, achievements)
Information about an upcoming event, including a map of the location
One member's personal story (with permission)
An email link to contact the organisation
A form to join the organisation
An interactive image slider with captions
A resource section with filter functionality (text, infographics and video resources)
Positive representations of the organisation and its members
Accessibility features
briefs.typographyHint: Friendly, rounded fonts for headings; clean body text. Avoid jargon — write for teenagers.
briefs.colourHint: Bright, energetic palette (e.g. teal, coral, sunshine yellow) with strong contrast for accessibility.

briefs.title: Local Sports & Fitness Club
briefs.scenario: A local multi-sport club wants a website that promotes its teams and fitness sessions. The club wants to grow its membership among 16-25 year olds and needs the site to showcase facilities, timetables and how to join.
briefs.purpose: To promote the club's teams, sessions and facilities and convert visitors into members.
briefs.targetAudience: 16- to 25-year-olds, including students new to the area
mustIncludes: Three pages
Drop-down menus (sports, sessions, membership)
Information about sports and fitness sessions
An accordion (e.g. frequently asked questions)
External links (e.g. national sport governing bodies)
A form to register interest in joining
Modal images (photo gallery with lightbox)
Video content with controls (session highlights)
Search functionality
Accessibility features
briefs.typographyHint: Strong condensed headings for a sporty energy; keep body text highly readable.
briefs.colourHint: High-contrast sport palette (e.g. royal blue and volt/highlighter accents) — check contrast ratios pass WCAG.
